title: Exploring Forces
subject: Science
description: Push and pull, effects of force, contact and non-contact forces (muscular, friction, magnetic, electrostatic, gravitational), weight vs mass, the spring balance, and buoyant force with floating and sinking.

questions.question: In science, what is the push or pull applied on an object generally called?
questions.explanation: The chapter defines force as the push or pull applied on an object. Weight is one particular force, motion is what a force can change, and charge is what builds up on rubbed objects.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of force and its symbol?
questions.explanation: The SI unit of force is the newton (written with a small 'n') and its symbol is N. Kilogram and gram are units of mass; the metre is a unit of length.

questions.question: According to the chapter, how many objects must interact, at the very least, for a force to come into play?
questions.explanation: A force is a push or pull on an object resulting from its interaction with ANOTHER object, so at least two objects must interact.

questions.question: Ragini says 'the wind is pushing me hard' while cycling against it. In this interaction, which two objects are involved?
options: Ragini's bicycle and the road surface
The Sun and the moving air around them
Ragini's legs and the bicycle pedals
The moving air and Ragini on her bicycle
questions.explanation: The wind (moving air) interacts with Ragini and her bicycle and pushes against them; that is why they must pedal harder. The other pairs are different interactions.

questions.question: If an object is at rest, it must mean that no force at all is acting on it.
questions.explanation: The 'A step further' box says an object at rest means the forces acting on it are balancing one another, not that there are no forces.

questions.question: A book lies at rest on a table. What does the chapter say about the forces acting on it?
options: The forces acting on it balance one another
No force of any kind acts on the book
Only friction is acting on the book
The forces on it keep changing direction
questions.explanation: Rest does not mean absence of force; it means the forces acting on the object balance each other. Balanced forces are studied in higher grades.

questions.question: When you push a table with your hand, which two objects are said to be interacting?
questions.explanation: The chapter's example: your hand is one object applying force on another object, the table; the two are interacting.

questions.question: When you push a table, the force you feel on your own hand disappears the moment you stop pushing.
questions.explanation: The box says that the moment you stopped pushing, the force on your hand disappeared - as soon as the interaction ceases, the force does too.

questions.question: Whenever two objects interact, which statement about the forces is correct?
options: Only the object that moves experiences a force
Only the heavier object experiences a force
Each object experiences a force from the other
The force stays even after the interaction ends
questions.explanation: Whenever two objects interact, each experiences a force from the other, and both forces vanish as soon as the interaction ceases.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT given in the chapter as an everyday example of applying a force?
questions.explanation: Opening a drawer, rolling a chapati and kicking a football are all listed as situations where a force is applied; quietly reading a book is not one of them.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements about force that agree with the chapter.
options: A force results from the interaction of at least two objects
The SI unit of force is the newton
A single isolated object can exert a force on itself
Force is the same thing as the mass of an object
A force can act only when two objects are touching
questions.explanation: Force needs at least two interacting objects and is measured in newton. An isolated object cannot exert force on itself, mass is not force, and non-contact forces act without touching.

questions.question: In Table 5.1, a friend holds your moving bicycle from behind to stop it. What effect of force is this?
options: Changing the shape of the bicycle frame
Stopping or decreasing the speed of the bicycle
Changing the direction of the bicycle
Making the bicycle start moving from rest
questions.explanation: Table 5.1 lists this action as a pull whose effect is stopping or decreasing the speed of the bicycle.

questions.question: Holding a moving bicycle from behind to stop it is classified in Table 5.1 as which kind of force?
options: A push and then a pull
Neither a push nor a pull
questions.explanation: Table 5.1 marks 'your friend holding your moving bicycle from behind to stop it' as a Pull.

questions.question: Hitting a moving ball with a bat is listed in Table 5.1 with which effect?
options: Changing the shape of the moving ball
Bringing the moving ball fully to rest
Reducing the mass of the moving ball
Changing the direction of the moving ball
questions.explanation: Table 5.1: hitting a moving ball with a bat is a push that changes the direction of the moving ball.

questions.question: What effect of force is shown when you press an inflated balloon?
options: A change in the shape of the balloon
A change in the speed of the balloon
A change in the mass of the balloon
A change in the colour of the balloon
questions.explanation: Table 5.1 lists pressing an inflated balloon as a push whose effect is a change in shape.

questions.question: Select ALL the effects that, according to the chapter, a force applied on an object may produce.
options: Make an object move from rest
Change the speed of a moving object
Change the direction of motion of an object
Change the amount of matter in the object
Change the colour of the object
Change the material the object is made of
questions.explanation: A force may make an object move from rest, change its speed, change its direction of motion, or change its shape. It does not change the amount of matter, colour or material.

questions.question: Rolling a chapati with a rolling pin mainly shows which effect of force?
options: A change in the speed of the dough
A change in the shape of the dough
A change in the direction of the dough
The dough starting to move from rest
questions.explanation: Rolling flattens and spreads the dough - the force changes its shape.

questions.question: A force can bring about a change in the shape of an object.
questions.explanation: Changing shape is one of the listed effects of force, e.g. pressing a balloon or rolling a chapati.

questions.question: A force can change either the speed or the direction of a moving object, but never both at the same time.
questions.explanation: The Snapshots say force can change an object's speed, direction of motion, or both. A force may cause some or all of its effects together.

questions.question: A fielder catches a fast-moving cricket ball and holds it. The main effect of the fielder's force on the ball is to
questions.explanation: Stopping a moving ball means its speed is reduced to zero - a change in speed. The ball's shape and mass are not what the force is changing here.

questions.question: Which statement about the effects of force is NOT correct?
options: A force can make a resting object start to move
A force always causes all its effects at once
A force can change the direction in which an object moves
A force can change the shape of an object
questions.explanation: A force may cause some OR all of its effects - not always all of them together. The other three are listed effects of force.

questions.question: A ball rolling on flat ground slows down and stops even though nobody touches it. What does the chapter conclude from this?
options: No force is acting; it stops on its own
The mass of the ball is decreasing
The ball's weight pulls it backwards
Some force must be acting on the ball
questions.explanation: Since a force is essential to change speed, and the speed decreases, some force must be acting - it turns out to be friction.

questions.question: Which action by Sonali and Ragini during their ride is an example of force changing the DIRECTION of motion?
options: Turning the handles to pass the herd of sheep
Pressing the bicycle bells near the sheep herd
Pumping air into the bicycle tyres at home
Enjoying the view from the top of the hill
questions.explanation: Turning the handles changes the direction of the bicycle. Pumping air changes the tyre's shape, and pressing a bell does not alter the ride's direction.

questions.question: Select the TWO situations in which the force changes the SHAPE of the object.
questions.explanation: Pressing a balloon and rolling a chapati change shape. Stopping a ball and braking change speed; turning a handle changes direction.

questions.question: Forces that act only when there is physical contact between the objects are called
questions.explanation: The chapter defines contact forces as forces that act only when there is physical contact between the objects, e.g. muscular force and friction.

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-contact force?
questions.explanation: A magnet exerts force from a distance, so magnetic force is a non-contact force. Muscular force, friction and pushing with a stick all need contact.

questions.question: Select the TWO contact forces named in the chapter.
questions.explanation: Muscular force and friction need physical contact. Magnetic, gravitational and electrostatic forces act from a distance (non-contact).

questions.question: Select ALL the non-contact forces described in the chapter.
questions.explanation: Magnetic, gravitational and electrostatic forces act without contact. Muscular force and friction need contact; buoyant force is applied by a liquid touching the object.

questions.question: Pushing a heavy box with a long stick is best described as
options: a non-contact force at a distance
a gravitational force on the box
an electrostatic force on the box
questions.explanation: Contact can be direct (hands) or indirect (a stick or rope). A stick still makes physical contact with the box, so it is a contact force.

questions.question: A force applied on a bucket through a rope is a non-contact force because your hand never touches the bucket.
questions.explanation: The chapter says contact can be indirect, through a stick or rope. The rope touches the bucket, so it is still a contact force.

questions.question: Which statement about contact and non-contact forces is NOT correct?
options: Two magnets must touch for magnetic force to act
Contact forces need the objects to be touching
Non-contact forces can act from a distance
Friction is one of the types of contact force
questions.explanation: Magnetic force is a non-contact force - a magnet exerts force on another magnet without touching it (Activity 5.5). The other statements are correct.

questions.question: Gravitational force is a contact force because falling objects eventually touch the ground.
questions.explanation: Gravitational force acts on an object without the Earth being in contact with it, so it is a non-contact force.

questions.question: Which pair consists of TWO non-contact forces?
questions.explanation: Magnetic and electrostatic forces both act from a distance. Each other pair contains at least one contact force (muscular or frictional).

questions.question: According to the Snapshots, forces can act
questions.explanation: The Snapshots state 'Forces can act with or without contact', covering contact and non-contact forces.

questions.question: A ball thrown upward is no longer touching anything, yet a force acts on it. Which force?
questions.explanation: Gravity is a non-contact force - the Earth pulls the ball down even though nothing touches it.

questions.question: A compass needle turns to point North. Which force is at work, and is it contact or non-contact?
questions.explanation: Exercise Q1 matches 'a compass needle pointing North' with magnetic force, which acts without contact.

questions.question: The force resulting from the action of muscles in our body is called
questions.explanation: The chapter names the force caused by the action of muscles - in walking, lifting, jumping - as muscular force.

questions.question: Muscular force occurs when muscles
questions.explanation: The text says muscular force occurs when muscles contract and elongate while doing any activity.

questions.question: Which process inside the body is given as an example of muscular force?
options: Pushing food through the alimentary canal
Light entering the eye to form an image
Hair growing longer over several weeks
questions.explanation: The 'Ever heard of' box says muscular force helps us chew food and push it through the alimentary canal during digestion.

questions.question: The expansion and contraction of heart muscles that circulate blood is an example of muscular force.
questions.explanation: The box states that expansion and contraction of heart muscles allows blood to circulate - a use of muscular force essential for survival.

questions.question: Select the TWO body functions the chapter mentions as using muscular force.
questions.explanation: The 'Ever heard of' box mentions chewing food, pushing food through the alimentary canal and the heart's muscles circulating blood.

questions.question: A child lifting a school bag is an example of which type of force?
questions.explanation: Exercise Q1 matches 'a child lifting a school bag' with muscular force - the child's muscles do the lifting.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed in the chapter as an activity caused by muscular force?
questions.explanation: Walking, running, lifting, pushing, jumping and stretching are listed. Floating still is explained by buoyant force, not by muscle action.

questions.question: Birds flying, fish swimming and insects crawling all move using which force?
questions.explanation: Animals, birds, fish and insects use muscular force for movement and survival (Fig. 5.3).

questions.question: When you lift a heavy bag with your muscles, which other force must your muscular force work against?
questions.explanation: The Earth pulls the bag downward (its weight); your muscular force must pull upward against this gravitational force.

questions.question: The force that comes into play when an object moves or tries to move over another surface is called
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's definition of friction - it arises when one surface moves or tries to move over another.

questions.question: In which direction does friction act on a sliding object?
options: Straight up, away from the surface
Towards the centre of the Earth
Opposite to the direction of motion
questions.explanation: Friction always acts opposite to the direction in which the object is moving or trying to move.

questions.question: According to the chapter, friction arises because of
options: irregularities in the surfaces in contact
static charges on the two surfaces
magnetic poles in the two surfaces
the Earth pulling the object down
questions.explanation: Friction arises due to irregularities in the two surfaces; they lock into each other and oppose motion of one surface over the other.

questions.question: Even surfaces that appear smooth have a large number of minute irregularities.
questions.explanation: Fig. 5.6 and the text explain that even apparently smooth surfaces have many minute irregularities that cause friction.

questions.question: In Activity 5.4 the same object, pushed the same way, stops at different distances on glass, cloth, wood, tile and sand. What is concluded?
options: Friction is the same for all surfaces
Friction depends on the nature of the surfaces
The object's weight changes on each surface
Friction acts only on rough surfaces
questions.explanation: Different stopping distances on different surfaces show that the force of friction depends on the nature of the surfaces in contact.

questions.question: If the same object is pushed with the same force, on which surface would you expect it to slide the FARTHEST?
questions.explanation: Friction is greater on rough surfaces, so the object stops soonest on rough surfaces and travels farthest on the smooth glass.

questions.question: Due to friction, the speed of a ball rolling on flat ground increases.
questions.explanation: Friction opposes motion, so it DEcreases the speed of the rolling ball until it stops (Exercise Q2 (ii) is False).

questions.question: Why do we sometimes slip on smooth surfaces like ice or polished floors?
options: Smooth surfaces exert a stronger pull of gravity
Smooth surfaces push our feet upward strongly
Smooth surfaces give our feet very little friction
questions.explanation: Friction depends on the nature of surfaces and is small on smooth ones; with little friction to oppose sliding, our feet slip.

questions.question: A ball released from point P rolls down an incline and stops at point A on a horizontal surface. How could you make it stop BEFORE reaching A when released from the same point?
options: Polish the surface until it shines
Pour a little oil on the surface
questions.explanation: A rougher surface increases friction, so the ball loses speed faster and stops earlier. Smoothing or oiling would reduce friction and let it go farther.

questions.question: For the same ball released from point P, which change would make it stop AFTER crossing point A?
options: Spread a layer of sand on the horizontal surface
Replace the horizontal surface with a smoother one
Cover the horizontal surface with rough cloth
Make the horizontal surface much rougher
questions.explanation: Less friction means less opposition to motion, so on a smoother surface the ball travels farther and crosses A.

questions.question: Friction acts only on objects that are already moving, never on an object that is merely trying to move.
questions.explanation: The definition says friction acts when an object moves OR tries to move over another surface, opposite to the direction in which it is moving or trying to move.

questions.question: Why are aeroplanes, ships, boats and high-speed trains designed with specific shapes?
options: To increase friction so they can stop quickly
To make them heavier and more stable
To reduce the gravitational pull on them
To cut down friction from the air or water
questions.explanation: Air and water exert friction on objects moving through them, so these vehicles are shaped to reduce that friction.

questions.question: Liquids and gases do not exert any force of friction on objects moving through them.
questions.explanation: The 'A step further' box says air, water and other liquids also exert force of friction on objects moving through them.

questions.question: In Activity 5.3 the object is pushed one way and then in the opposite direction; it stops both times. What does this tell us about friction?
options: It acts only when the object moves to the right
It opposes motion in whichever direction it slides
It acts in the same direction as the push
It stops acting once the direction is reversed
questions.explanation: Whichever direction the object slides, friction acts opposite to that motion and brings it to rest.

questions.question: Friction is greater on which kind of surface?
questions.explanation: The chapter concludes 'Friction is greater on rough surfaces'.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements about friction that are correct.
options: It opposes the motion of the object
It acts along the direction of motion
It can act from a distance
It is always attractive like gravity
questions.explanation: Friction opposes motion and is a contact force arising from surfaces touching. It does not act along the motion or from a distance.

questions.question: A cricket ball rolling across the field stops on its own just before the boundary. Which force stopped it?
questions.explanation: Exercise Q1 matches 'a cricket ball stopping on its own just before the boundary line' with frictional force.

questions.question: In Activity 5.4, what is deliberately CHANGED between trials while the object and the push are kept the same?
options: The surface the object slides on
The size of the object being pushed
The mass of the pushed object
questions.explanation: The variable tested is the nature of the surface (glass, cloth, wood, tile, sand); object and push are kept the same so stopping distance reflects friction.

questions.question: Predict: the same lunch box, given the same push, on a ceramic tile and then on sand. What will happen?
options: It travels farther on sand than on the tile
It goes farther on the tile than on the sand
It travels the same distance on both
It does not move at all on the smooth tile
questions.explanation: Sand is rougher than tile and offers more friction, so the box stops sooner on sand.

questions.question: Which statement about friction is NOT correct?
options: Friction is lower on smoother surfaces
Friction opposes the direction of motion
Friction is completely absent on glass
Friction is a type of contact force
questions.explanation: Glass is smooth but still has minute irregularities, so friction is small, not zero - the object still stops eventually. The other statements are correct.

questions.question: Select the TWO changes that would REDUCE the friction on a sliding object.
options: Streamlining the object's shape when moving through air
Pushing the object in the opposite direction
questions.explanation: Smoother surfaces have fewer irregularities, and streamlined shapes reduce friction from air/water. Sand or rough cloth increase friction; reversing the push does not reduce it.

questions.question: The force exerted by a magnet on another magnet or a magnetic material is called
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's definition of magnetic force, a non-contact force.

questions.question: When like poles of two magnets (North-North or South-South) are brought close, they
questions.explanation: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

questions.question: Unlike poles of two magnets (North-South) brought close together will
questions.explanation: Unlike poles (North-South) attract each other.

questions.question: In Activity 5.5 the upper ring magnet floats above the lower one. If you now flip BOTH magnets over, what happens?
options: It drops, because unlike poles now face each other
It flies right off the top end of the wooden stick
It still floats; like poles still face each other
It stops behaving like a magnet from then on
questions.explanation: Flipping both magnets keeps like poles facing each other, so they still repel and the upper magnet keeps floating.

questions.question: When you push the floating ring magnet down gently and feel a force on it, this demonstrates that
options: a magnet needs contact to act
the stick is pushing the magnet up
questions.explanation: You feel the repulsion between the magnets even though they are not in contact - a non-contact force.

questions.question: Magnetic force can be either attractive or repulsive.
questions.explanation: Unlike poles attract and like poles repel; the chapter contrasts this with gravity, which is only attractive.

questions.question: A magnet can exert a force on a magnetic material only after it touches the material.
questions.explanation: A magnet exerts force on another magnet or a magnetic material from a distance, which is why magnetic force is a non-contact force.

questions.question: Why does the chapter mention electromagnets while discussing magnetic force?
options: They are a type of friction
questions.explanation: The chapter recalls that electromagnets, studied earlier, behave like magnets and so exert magnetic force too.

questions.question: Select the TWO correct statements about magnets.
options: A magnet attracts objects made of magnetic materials
A magnet attracts objects of every material
Magnets must touch an object to exert force
questions.explanation: Like poles repel and magnets attract magnetic materials. They do not attract everything, act without contact, and unlike poles attract.

questions.question: Which of these pairs will REPEL each other?
options: A magnet and an iron nail
questions.explanation: Only like poles repel. N-S or S-N attract, and a magnet attracts a nail made of magnetic material.

questions.question: In which Grade 6 chapter of Curiosity did students first learn about magnets?
questions.explanation: The text refers back to the chapter 'Exploring Magnets' in Curiosity, Grade 6.

questions.question: A plastic scale rubbed with polythene is brought near small pieces of paper. What happens?
options: The paper pieces are pushed away from the scale
The paper pieces catch fire and burn away
Nothing at all happens to the paper pieces
The paper pieces are pulled to it and stick
questions.explanation: The paper pieces get pulled towards the charged scale and stick to it - electrostatic attraction.

questions.question: Charges that build up on rubbed surfaces and do not move by themselves are called
questions.explanation: They are called static charges because they do not move by themselves.

questions.question: The two kinds of static charges are called
questions.explanation: The chapter says the two kinds of static charges are said to be 'positive' and 'negative'. North and south are magnetic poles.

questions.question: Two balloons rubbed with a woollen cloth are brought near each other. What happens?
options: They move together and stick fast
They stay exactly where they were
They move apart from each other
They start spinning round and round
questions.explanation: Both balloons acquire similar charges, and like charges repel, so they move apart (Exercise Q3).

questions.question: Why do two balloons rubbed with the same woollen cloth repel each other?
options: Both get opposite charges and unlike charges repel
Rubbing turns them into magnets with like poles
The air between them pushes them apart
Both get similar charges and like charges repel
questions.explanation: Charged in the same way, the balloons acquire similar charges; the chapter infers that like charges repel.

questions.question: When the woollen cloth used for rubbing is brought near a rubbed balloon, they
options: repel, as they carry similar charges
neither attract nor repel at all
questions.explanation: The rubbing and rubbed objects acquire opposite kinds of charge, and unlike charges attract.

questions.question: There is no force between two charged objects placed a small distance apart.
questions.explanation: Charged objects exert electrostatic force on each other even without contact - they attract or repel (Exercise Q2 (iii) is False).

questions.question: The force exerted by a charged body on another charged body or an uncharged body is called
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's definition of electrostatic force, a non-contact force.

questions.question: Electrostatic force is a non-contact force.
questions.explanation: The force between charged bodies comes into play even when the objects are not in contact.

questions.question: Which precaution does Activity 5.6 give after rubbing the plastic scale?
options: Heat the scale gently before use
Wet the paper pieces before testing
Do not touch the rubbed part
Rub the scale again with a metal spoon
questions.explanation: The activity says: do not touch the rubbed part with your hand or any metal object, and do not touch the paper pieces.

questions.question: The charged scale attracts UNCHARGED paper pieces. What does this show about electrostatic force?
options: It acts only between two charged objects
It acts only on magnetic materials
It acts only on metal objects
It acts on charged and uncharged objects
questions.explanation: A charged object attracts uncharged objects made of certain materials, such as paper - so electrostatic force acts on uncharged bodies too.

questions.question: After rubbing, the rubbing object and the rubbed object acquire
questions.explanation: Both get charged but with opposite kinds of charge - which is why the cloth and balloon attract.

questions.question: After rubbing a balloon with a woollen cloth, only the balloon becomes charged while the cloth stays uncharged.
questions.explanation: Both the rubbing object (cloth) and the rubbed object (balloon) get charged, with opposite kinds of charge.

questions.question: A balloon rubbed on a woollen cloth attracts strands of hair. Which force is this?
questions.explanation: Exercise Q1 matches the rubbed balloon attracting hair strands with electrostatic force.

questions.question: Select the TWO inferences the chapter draws from the balloon experiments (Activity 5.7).
options: Charges flow between the balloons on their own
Only the woollen cloth gets charged
questions.explanation: Similarly charged balloons repelled (like charges repel) and the balloon and cloth attracted (unlike charges attract).

questions.question: According to the 'A step further' box, what do charges constitute when they move?
questions.explanation: Moving charges constitute an electric current - the same current that lights a lamp or produces heating and magnetic effects.

questions.question: Predict: a THIRD balloon that has NOT been rubbed is brought near a rubbed, charged balloon. What happens?
questions.explanation: A charged object attracts an uncharged object made of certain materials, so the charged balloon attracts the uncharged one.

questions.question: Static charges are so named because they keep moving across the surface of the charged object.
questions.explanation: They are called static because they do NOT move by themselves.

questions.question: The force with which the Earth attracts objects towards itself is called
questions.explanation: The Earth's attraction on objects is the gravitational force, also called force of gravity or simply gravity.

questions.question: Gravitational force is always
questions.explanation: Unlike magnetic and electrostatic forces, gravitational force is always attractive.

questions.question: Which forces can be EITHER attractive or repulsive?
questions.explanation: Magnetic and electrostatic forces can attract or repel; gravitational force is only attractive.

questions.question: Gravity is a non-contact force.
questions.explanation: The gravitational force acts without the Earth being in contact with the object it attracts.

questions.question: While a ball thrown vertically upward is going up, its speed
questions.explanation: Under gravity the upward speed decreases until the ball momentarily stops at the top.

questions.question: What happens to a ball at the topmost point of its vertical throw?
options: It stays there until it is pushed
It keeps moving up but slowly
It moves sideways in the air
questions.explanation: The ball slows, stops momentarily at the top, changes direction and falls straight down.

questions.question: A ball is thrown upward. At its topmost position, which force acts on it and in which direction?
options: No force, since the ball is at rest
questions.explanation: Even when momentarily at rest at the top, the Earth's gravitational pull acts downward - that is what makes the ball come back down.

questions.question: While the ball moves DOWNWARD, in which direction does the friction of the air act on it?
options: Air exerts no friction on it
questions.explanation: Air exerts friction on objects moving through it, and friction acts opposite to the direction of motion - so upward while the ball falls.

questions.question: An object is in non-uniform motion (its speed or direction keeps changing). Is a force acting on it?
options: Yes - no such change happens without a force
No - motion needs no force once started
Only if the object is moving downward
Only if the object touches something
questions.explanation: The chapter states that a change in speed or direction never takes place without the action of a force (Exercise Q8).

questions.question: When an object is dropped from a height, what path does it take?
options: A curved path to one side
questions.explanation: Fig. 5.11(a): a dropped object takes a straight vertical path downwards before touching the ground.

questions.question: While the thrown ball is coming back down, its speed
questions.explanation: During the downward part of vertical motion the speed goes on increasing under gravity.

questions.question: A ripe fruit falls from a tree. Which force is responsible?
questions.explanation: Exercise Q1 matches 'a fruit falling from a tree' with gravitational force.

questions.question: In vertical motion, the direction of a thrown ball's motion changes at its topmost point.
questions.explanation: The ball moves up, stops momentarily, and its direction of motion changes to downward.

questions.question: Which statement about gravitational force is NOT correct?
options: It can repel very light objects
It is always an attractive force
It pulls objects towards the Earth
questions.explanation: Gravity is always attractive, for every object. The other three statements are from the chapter.

questions.question: Select the TWO correct statements about a ball thrown vertically upward.
options: Its speed decreases while going up
Its speed increases while coming down
It stops permanently at the top
questions.explanation: Speed decreases going up and increases coming down; the direction changes at the top, where the stop is only momentary.

questions.question: An object moving straight up or down under the influence of gravity is said to undergo
questions.explanation: The chapter calls motion in a vertical direction under the influence of gravitational force 'vertical motion'.

questions.question: The weight of an object is defined as
options: the amount of matter it is made of
the amount of space it takes up
the speed at which it falls down
the force with which Earth pulls it
questions.explanation: Weight is the force with which the Earth pulls an object towards itself; mass is the amount of matter.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of weight?
questions.explanation: Weight is a force, so its SI unit is the newton (N), like any other force.

questions.question: Mass is
options: the pull of the Earth on an object
the amount of matter in an object
the stretch of a spring balance
the upward push from a liquid
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in grams or kilograms.

questions.question: Mass is measured in which units?
questions.explanation: Mass is measured in grams (g) or kilograms (kg); newton is the unit of force/weight.

questions.question: Which of these can change from place to place?
questions.explanation: Weight can vary because gravitational force varies, but mass stays the same everywhere.

questions.question: The weight of an object on the Moon is about one-sixth of its weight on the Earth. What causes this?
options: The Moon's gravitational pull is weaker
The object loses some matter on the Moon
questions.explanation: Weight depends on the gravitational force, which is much smaller on the Moon; the object's mass is unchanged (Exercise Q9).

questions.question: Does the MASS of an object also become one-sixth when taken to the Moon?
options: No, the mass stays the same
Only if the object is heavy
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change with place; only weight changes (Exercise Q9).

questions.question: From the chapter's table, a 1 kg object weighs 10 N on Earth. What is its weight on the Moon?
questions.explanation: The table gives 1.6 N on the Moon; 3.8 N is Mars, 9 N is Venus and 25.4 N is Jupiter.

questions.question: On which body in the chapter's table does a 1 kg object have the GREATEST weight?
questions.explanation: Jupiter: 25.4 N, more than Earth (10 N), Venus (9 N) and Mars (3.8 N).

questions.question: According to the table, what is the weight of a 1 kg object on Venus?
questions.explanation: The table lists 9 N on Venus; 10 N is Earth, 3.8 N is Mars and 1.6 N is the Moon.

questions.question: An object weighs 20 N on Earth. Using the chapter's table (1 kg: 10 N on Earth, 1.6 N on Moon), what would it weigh on the Moon?
questions.explanation: 20 N on Earth means a mass of 2 kg; on the Moon each kg weighs 1.6 N, so 2 x 1.6 = 3.2 N. (7.6 N would be Mars, 18 N Venus, 50.8 N Jupiter.)

questions.question: Using the table (1 kg weighs 3.8 N on Mars), what is the weight of a 2 kg object on Mars?
questions.explanation: 2 kg x 3.8 N per kg = 7.6 N. 3.2 N would be on the Moon, 20 N on Earth and 18 N on Venus.

questions.question: A 1 kg object has a mass of 1 kg on the Earth, on the Moon and on Jupiter alike.
questions.explanation: The table shows the mass staying 1 kg everywhere while the weight differs - mass does not change with place.

questions.question: Saying 'the weight of the wheat bag is 10 kg' is scientifically correct.
questions.explanation: Kilogram is a unit of mass; in scientific use weight must be given in newton. The chapter says the everyday usage is not correct scientifically.

questions.question: Why can the weight of an object differ very slightly at different places on the Earth?
options: The object's mass changes slightly with place
Friction is different at different places
Air pressure changes the weight of objects
Gravitational pull varies slightly across Earth
questions.explanation: The chapter says gravitational force can vary very slightly from place to place on Earth, so weight can change while mass does not.

questions.question: Why is it acceptable, for practical purposes, to 'weigh' an object to find its mass?
options: Weight stays almost the same everywhere on Earth
Weight and mass are the same quantity
Mass cannot be measured in any other way
Weight is measured in kilograms anyway
questions.explanation: Since weight remains almost the same everywhere on the Earth, measuring weight gives a reliable indication of mass.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements about MASS that are correct.
options: It stays the same at every place
It is measured in grams or kilograms
It becomes smaller on the Moon
It is a kind of force
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter, measured in g or kg, and is the same everywhere. Weight, not mass, is a force in newton that changes on the Moon.

questions.question: Which statement about mass and weight is NOT correct?
options: Mass is the amount of matter in an object
Weight can differ on different planets
questions.explanation: Mass is measured in grams or kilograms; it is weight (a force) that is measured in newton.

questions.question: Which simple device does the chapter use to measure weight?
questions.explanation: A spring balance measures weight (force); a beam balance compares masses.

questions.question: How does a spring balance indicate the weight of an object hung from its hook?
options: By the colour the spring turns
By the amount the spring stretches
By how fast the object falls
By the sound the spring makes
questions.explanation: When an object is hung from the hook the spring stretches, and the amount of stretching gives the weight.

questions.question: What is the range of the spring balance shown in Fig. 5.13?
questions.explanation: Activity 5.10: the maximum weight it can measure is 10 N, so its range is 0 to 10 N.

questions.question: On the Fig. 5.13 balance, the bigger marks are 1 N apart with 5 small divisions between them. What is the smallest weight it can read?
questions.explanation: One small division = 1 N / 5 = 0.2 N, so the smallest reading is 0.2 N.

questions.question: A different spring balance has bigger marks 2 N apart with 4 small divisions between them. What is its smallest reading?
questions.explanation: Smallest reading = difference between big marks / number of divisions = 2 N / 4 = 0.5 N.

questions.question: A spring balance has bigger marks 1 N apart and 10 small divisions between them. One small division represents
questions.explanation: 1 N / 10 divisions = 0.1 N per small division.

questions.question: Why should you not hang an object heavier than the maximum value a spring balance can measure?
options: The spring balance may get damaged
The reading will be too accurate
questions.explanation: Activity 5.12 warns that objects heavier than the maximum may damage the spring balance.

questions.question: The gram scale on a spring balance is marked assuming the balance is used on the Earth.
questions.explanation: The mass values were marked assuming the balance is used on Earth with Earth's gravitational force attracting the object.

questions.question: A spring balance can measure any weight, however large, as long as the object is hung carefully.
questions.explanation: Each spring balance has a range (e.g. 0-10 N); heavier objects may damage it.

questions.question: In Activity 5.9 different objects stretch the spring by different amounts. What does this indicate?
options: The spring changes its own nature every time
All the objects have exactly the same weight
The spring is being affected by a hidden magnet
Earth pulls different objects with different forces
questions.explanation: Different stretches show that the Earth pulls different objects with different forces - their weights differ.

questions.question: In Activity 5.9, which quantity is CHANGED from trial to trial, while the spring and nail stay the same?
options: The object hung from the spring
The length of the unstretched spring
The nail the spring hangs from
The place where the activity is done
questions.explanation: Objects of different masses (pencil box, tiffin box, stone) are hung one by one; the resulting stretch is what is observed.

questions.question: Why would the gram (mass) scale of a spring balance NOT give correct values if used far from Earth?
options: Springs stop stretching away from the Earth
It was marked using Earth's gravitational pull
Mass itself changes when away from the Earth
The hook becomes weightless and falls off
questions.explanation: The mass values are marked assuming the Earth's gravitational force acts; elsewhere the pull differs, so the stretch would not match the marked mass.

questions.question: On the Fig. 5.13 balance (0.2 N per small division), the pointer rests 3 small divisions past the 4 N mark. What is the reading?
questions.explanation: 3 divisions x 0.2 N = 0.6 N beyond 4 N, giving 4.6 N.

questions.question: How is the smallest value a spring balance can read worked out?
options: Multiply the range by the number of divisions
Divide the big-mark gap by the number of divisions
Count the total number of bigger marks on the scale
Read off the largest number printed on the scale
questions.explanation: Activity 5.11: weight difference between two bigger marks (1 N) divided by the number of small divisions (5) gives 0.2 N.

questions.question: Select the TWO things you must check before using an unfamiliar spring balance.
options: Its range (the maximum weight it can measure)
The value of its smallest division
The brand name printed on it
questions.explanation: The chapter says ranges and smallest divisions differ between balances, so always look carefully at the instrument before use.

questions.question: The force applied by a liquid on an object in the upward direction is known as
questions.explanation: The chapter names the upward force from a liquid 'upthrust or buoyant force'.

questions.question: When you push a tightly closed empty bottle into a bucket of water, what do you feel?
options: A downward pull on the bottle
No force at all on the bottle
An upward push on the bottle
questions.explanation: Activity 5.13: you feel an upward push, showing water applies an upward force on the bottle.

questions.question: An object placed in a liquid SINKS when
options: gravitational force exceeds the buoyant force
buoyant force exceeds the gravitational force
the two forces are exactly equal
no gravitational force acts on it
questions.explanation: If the gravitational force is more than the buoyant force, the object sinks; if equal, it floats.

questions.question: An object FLOATS in a liquid when
options: gravity and buoyant force are equal
the object has no mass at all
questions.explanation: The chapter says if the two forces are equal, the object floats.

questions.question: The chapter mentions one factor that buoyant force depends on. Which is it?
questions.explanation: One factor on which buoyant force depends is the density of the liquid (studied in a later chapter).

questions.question: According to Archimedes' Principle, the upward force on an immersed object equals
options: the weight of the object itself
the mass of the liquid in the container
the weight of the liquid it displaces
questions.explanation: Archimedes discovered that an immersed object experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces.

questions.question: A coin sinks in water but a bigger wooden block floats. Which explanation matches the chapter?
options: Coin: weight exceeds upthrust; block: weight equals upthrust
The coin is heavier than the block, so only it sinks
The block is bigger, and big objects always float
Water pushes the coin down but pushes the block up
questions.explanation: An object sinks when gravity exceeds the buoyant force and floats when they are equal. The block displaces water equal to its weight; the coin does not (Exercise Q4).

questions.question: Why can the rock pumice float on water?
options: It is made of an unusually light metal
Trapped gas makes it less dense than water
It becomes electrically charged in water
It repels water by magnetic force
questions.explanation: Pumice forms when gas-rich lava cools quickly, trapping bubbles; the porous rock is less dense than water and floats.

questions.question: All liquids apply an upward force on objects placed in them.
questions.explanation: The chapter says all liquids apply a similar upward force (buoyant force), not only water.

questions.question: A mug feels lighter inside a bucket of water because the water pushes it upward.
questions.explanation: The buoyant force of the water acts upward on the mug, making it feel lighter.

questions.question: An object floats whenever its weight is greater than the weight of the liquid it displaces.
questions.explanation: By Archimedes' Principle, if the weight of displaced liquid is smaller than the object's weight the object SINKS; it floats when they are equal.

questions.question: Three objects of the same size and shape but different materials float in water, dipping to different depths. Which is the heaviest?
options: It cannot be told from depth
questions.explanation: A floating object's weight equals the weight of water it displaces; dipping deeper displaces more water, so the deepest one is heaviest (Exercise Q10, reasoning from Archimedes' Principle).

questions.question: Select the TWO forces acting on an object placed in a liquid, as described in the chapter.
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls the object down while the liquid applies an upward buoyant force; their comparison decides floating or sinking.

questions.question: Which statement about buoyant force is NOT correct?
options: An object sinks if buoyant force exceeds gravity
Buoyant force acts upward on the object
Buoyant force depends on the liquid's density
Buoyant force is also called upthrust
questions.explanation: It is the other way round: an object sinks when gravitational force exceeds the buoyant force.

questions.question: You release a closed empty bottle that you had pushed under water. What happens?
options: It sinks slowly to the bottom
It stays where you released it
It bounces back up to the surface
It spins but does not rise
questions.explanation: Activity 5.13: on release the bottle bounces back to the surface because of the upward force from the water.

questions.question: Buoyant force is listed in the chapter's Snapshots as one of the non-contact forces.
questions.explanation: The Snapshots list magnetic, gravitational and electrostatic as non-contact forces; buoyant force is the upward force applied by a liquid in contact with the object.

questions.question: Why does it feel harder to pedal a bicycle uphill than on flat ground?
options: Friction disappears on slopes, so pedalling is wasted
The bicycle's mass increases as it climbs
Air exerts no friction while going uphill
Gravity pulls the bicycle down the slope
questions.explanation: The Earth's gravitational pull acts on the bicycle; on a slope part of this pull acts against the climb, so the rider must push the pedals harder.

questions.question: A boat gradually slows down after its engine is switched off. Which force causes this?
questions.explanation: Water exerts friction on objects moving through it, opposing their motion and slowing them.

questions.question: A comb run through dry hair attracts tiny bits of paper. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Rubbing charges the comb, and a charged object attracts uncharged pieces of paper - electrostatic force.

questions.question: Which pair of quantities are BOTH measured in newton?
questions.explanation: Weight is a force, so both are measured in newton; mass is measured in grams or kilograms.

questions.question: Select the TWO actions from Table 5.1 that are classified as a PUSH.
options: Hitting a moving ball with a bat
A friend holding your moving bicycle from behind
questions.explanation: Table 5.1 marks hitting a ball and pressing a balloon as pushes; holding a bicycle from behind is a pull, as are opening a drawer and stretching a band.

questions.question: Sonali and Ragini's bicycles sped downhill without pedalling. Which TWO forces were acting on the moving bicycles along the slope?
options: Gravity down the slope and friction against motion
Magnetic force and electrostatic force together
Muscular force and the buoyant force of air
Only gravity, with no friction acting at all
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls the bicycles down the slope while friction from the road and air acts opposite to their motion.

questions.question: A step-by-step chain: rubbing a balloon with wool -> ? -> balloon sticks to a wall. Fill in the missing step.
options: Static charges build up on it
questions.explanation: Rubbing certain materials builds up static charges; the charged balloon then attracts uncharged objects like the wall.

questions.question: Which of the following is a FALSE statement about the forces in this chapter?
options: Friction can act on an object moving through air
A charged object can attract an uncharged object
Gravitational force can repel objects from Earth
Like magnetic poles repel each other
questions.explanation: Gravity is always attractive. Air friction, attraction of uncharged objects by charged ones, and like poles repelling are all correct.

questions.question: A spring balance reads 5 N when a stone hangs from it. What does this 5 N represent?
questions.explanation: A spring balance's newton scale shows weight - the force with which the Earth pulls the stone.

questions.question: A student says: 'The wind pushed us, so wind force must be a non-contact force like gravity.' What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Moving air touches the rider, so it is a contact force
Wind is actually a form of magnetic force acting
Gravity is a contact force, so the comparison fails
Wind cannot apply any force at all on a rider
questions.explanation: The air physically pushes against the rider's body; air exerts friction and pushes through contact. Non-contact forces (gravity, magnetic, electrostatic) act from a distance.

questions.question: Pressing a bicycle bell and kicking a football are both examples of applying a push.
questions.explanation: Pressing and kicking are pushes applied by muscular force.

questions.question: Select the TWO forces that act on a rubbed balloon floating still in a bucket of water (ignore air).
options: Frictional force from the bucket's air
questions.explanation: Gravity acts downward on any object; the water applies an upward buoyant force. Water is not magnetic and a balloon has no muscles.
